criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale. Include the following required information: What is the spacecraft's primary mission? Why is the mission needed? How many spacecraft are used and why? Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: Primary mission, rationale (bleaching, fluid lensing), single-spacecraft choice and customers are all addressed with reasoned detail. The operator is vague ('operated and accessed from Australia ground facilities') and funding is speculative. Introduction references are present, but the bibliography is URL-only and incomplete, so referencing is only partly adequate.

evidence.quote: Thus, only one satellite is required.

criteria.name: Main body: mission design. Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate. Include relevant screenshots and software files in the main body of the report and/or appendix. Include the following information: Where will it launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? Which ground control facilities will you use? How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: Strengths: SSO inclination for 600 km (about 97.8°) checks out, and STK access data and orbit screenshots are provided. Weaknesses: equatorial-launch logic is inverted for a retrograde orbit; the Vega E is unbuilt; the RAAN explanation is wrong; no local time of descending node, period or swath/GSD sizing; manoeuvre statements contradict; no decay analysis; EOL drag-sail text is truncated; the access table is mis-numbered.

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.reasoning: The conclusion draws some reasonable points, including the launch-vehicle risk and the ground-station choice. However, it largely restates the design without quantitative evidence such as contact durations, pass counts or EOL lifetime. It does not acknowledge the unresolved issues in the body, so it is somewhat generic.

evidence.quote: A polar sun-synchronous orbit allows for consistent illumination of the oceans while maintaining a constant sun angle.
A specific launch vehicle – the Vega E – has been selected although it has not been built yet.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Headings and a clear section structure with an executive summary are present, and most figures carry captions. Citations are seriously inconsistent: in-text numbers run to [74] but the bibliography lists only [1]–[10], [10] is used twice, entries are garbled, and Wikipedia is cited. Frequent grammar and typo errors, unnumbered tables and an uncaptioned Image 3 further reduce quality.

evidence.quote: It’s first launch will occur in 2024
construction of a Earth observation satellite

requirements.where: Orbit and Ground Control (Images 1–5); STK files not evident

technical_issues.issue: Equatorial launch is argued to be most efficient, but Earth-rotation benefit largely disappears for a retrograde ~98° orbit. Plane-change penalty from 5°N is not analysed.
RAAN is said to indicate the launch facility location. RAAN depends on launch time/epoch and site longitude; no epoch is given. Table also uses Earth radius 6371 km, inconsistent with STK's 6378 km.

Sun-synchronous daytime imaging is claimed but local time of descending node is never specified. Orbit period, swath width and ground sample distance are not calculated, so 600 km and 'daily' coverage are unsupported.
The only orbital manoeuvre is said to occur at EOL, yet the satellite is stated to have no thrusters, so manoeuvre claims are contradictory.

A five-year life at 600 km with passive disposal is asserted without decay or lifetime analysis. STK run 2025–2030 is mentioned but no results are shown; executive summary cites perturbation calculations that are absent.
Drag-sail sentence is truncated ('to ‘ and is suitable...'), leaving the EOL description incomplete and the drag sail unsized.
Access table lists two entries numbered 13 and 14 rows in total despite text claiming fifteen periods; pass frequency per day is not stated explicitly.
Mount Pleasant radio telescopes are used as an Earth-observation downlink without frequency, link budget, data rate or antenna suitability justification.
Inclination-altitude plot has no source citation and appears to be borrowed material.
Wikipedia is used as a source ('Timeline of spaceflight'), which the task explicitly prohibits.
In-text citations run to [74] but only [1]–[10] are listed; [10] is used for both the Falcon 9 manifest and the drag-sail reference; entries [5] and [10] are garbled.

overall: Plausible single-satellite sun-synchronous concept with correct 600 km inclination (about 97.8°) and STK access analysis. However, launch reasoning is inverted for retrograde orbit, RAAN and manoeuvre statements are wrong or contradictory, EOL is truncated and unsupported, and citations are broken and include Wikipedia. Approximately 50% weighted.

feedback.summary: You have set out a clear, well-motivated single-satellite concept in the Introduction, with a sensible sun-synchronous inclination at 600 km and useful STK access analysis. The main gaps are in the technical reasoning: the launch-site argument needs revisiting for a retrograde orbit, the RAAN and manoeuvre statements need correcting, and the end-of-life and referencing need completing.
next_steps: Revisit the launch-site justification in Mission Design – Launch. For a retrograde ~98° orbit the Earth-rotation benefit of an equatorial site is much smaller, so explain why Vega E is still preferable, including the plane-change cost from 5°N.

Correct and complete the Orbit section: state the local time of descending node, orbital period, swath width and ground sample distance, and explain your RAAN and epoch. Make the manoeuvre statements consistent with a satellite that has no thrusters.

Finish Mission Duration & EOL with a decay or lifetime estimate supporting the five-year life, show the STK results, and complete the drag-sail description with its size. Replace the Wikipedia source with authoritative references and check every in-text citation against the bibliography.

criteria.C1: Your Introduction clearly states the primary mission, the bleaching and fluid-lensing rationale, why one spacecraft suffices, and the likely users. To reach Accomplished, name the operator precisely rather than 'Australia ground facilities', justify or remove the speculative funding comment, and replace the URL-only bibliography with full literature references.
criteria.C2: Your strongest evidence is the sun-synchronous inclination (about 97.8° at 600 km), the STK access analysis and the orbit screenshots. The launch reasoning and RAAN explanation are currently inverted or incorrect, and the manoeuvre claims contradict the no-thrust design. To reach Accomplished, support major requirements with calculations (period, swath, GSD, decay), correct these errors, and justify the Mount Pleasant downlink with frequency and data rate.
criteria.C3: Your conclusion makes sensible points about constant illumination and launch-vehicle risk, but it is largely generic. It does not cite quantitative results such as contact durations, pass counts or EOL lifetime. To reach Accomplished, summarise the key numbers from your analysis, state what they show, and acknowledge the remaining limitations.
criteria.C4: The report has a clear heading structure and an executive summary, and most figures are captioned. Citation consistency is the main weakness: in-text references run beyond the bibliography, one number is used for two sources, entries are garbled, and Wikipedia is cited. To reach Accomplished, fix every citation, label all tables and Image 3 consistently, and proofread for grammar and typos.
